subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Processing and Middlemen
description: A short lesson to help you apply Processing and Middlemen.

hook.text: Between the farmer and your cup, coffee passes through 6–10 middlemen. Each takes a cut.

buildup.text: After picking, cherries go to a processor, then an exporter, an importer, a roaster, a distributor, and a retailer.

discovery.text: Each step adds cost but also margin. The exporter and roaster capture the most value in the chain.

twist.text: Some cooperatives cut out middlemen by exporting directly. Farmers earn 2–3x more per kilogram this way.

climax.text: Direct trade movements try to shorten the chain—connecting roasters with farmers for better prices and quality.

punchline.text: Fewer hands in the chain, more money at the source.

quiz.question: How many middlemen typically stand between farmer and cup?

details.summary: Between the farmer and the roaster sit layers of middlemen: wet mill operators, dry mill processors, exporters, importers, and traders. Each takes a margin, and the farmer's share shrinks at every step. In many supply chains, the farmer receives less than 10 percent of the retail price.
details.whyItMatters: Middlemen provide necessary services but their cumulative margins mean farmers capture the smallest share. Shortening the chain returns more value to growers.
takeaways: Multiple middlemen sit between farmer and roaster
Each intermediary takes a margin from the final price
Farmers often receive less than 10 percent of retail price

faq.question: Why are there so many intermediaries in coffee trade?
faq.answer: Each intermediary serves a function: wet mills process cherries, dry mills sort and grade, exporters handle logistics and documentation, importers manage customs, and traders connect supply with demand. Not all can be eliminated, but consolidation through cooperatives reduces layers.

faq.question: How does direct trade reduce the middleman problem?
faq.answer: Direct trade connects roasters with farmers directly, cutting out exporters and importers. Roasters pay higher prices because savings from eliminating middlemen go to the farmer. It requires more logistics effort from the roaster but builds lasting relationships.
